title: CIA-UAP-D020, Memorandum on Unconventional Aircraft Sightings, 1955
what_is_it: A CIA Top Secret internal memorandum (with a Top Secret signature/cover routing sheet attached) summarising the debriefing of witnesses who reported an unconventional aerial sighting.
core_summary: A 1955 CIA memorandum records the debriefing of a group who observed a luminous object from a train inside the Soviet Union. The document concludes the sighting can probably be explained as steep-climbing aircraft or missiles, and that the evidence is not firm enough to conclude the Soviets have developed a radically new type of aircraft. It is dated 1 November 1955 and signed by H. H. Scoville, Jr. of the Office of Scientific Intelligence.
interpretation_warnings: Source text is heavily OCR-degraded; several body quotes are garbled reconstructions and should be checked against the original scan.
Witness identities (e.g. Senator Russell) and place names (Baku, Tiflis) come from the war.gov metadata, not from legible source text.
The document itself frames the sighting as an ordinary phenomenon (aircraft/missiles), not a confirmed UAP.
Single-source debriefing of eyewitness observers made from a moving train; no corroborating instrument data.

public_headline: 1955 CIA memo weighs Soviet train sighting of a luminous object
public_tldr: This is a two-page Top Secret internal memorandum from the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), dated 1 November 1955, summarising a debriefing of witnesses who reported seeing a luminous object from a moving train inside the Soviet Union. The memo concludes the sighting can probably be explained as steep-climbing aircraft or missiles, and that the available evidence is not firm enough to say the Soviets had built a radically new type of aircraft. It was signed by H. H. Scoville, Jr. of the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence.
public_narrative:
This document is an internal CIA memorandum marked Top Secret, running to two pages, with a Top Secret signature and cover routing sheet attached. It records a debriefing — an after-the-event interview — of a group of witnesses who reported an unusual sighting.

According to the memo, the witnesses observed a luminous object rising into the sky while travelling on a train inside the Soviet Union. War.gov's catalogue assigns the incident to 1955 in Azerbaijan, which was then part of the Soviet Union; the specific place names come from that catalogue rather than from clearly legible text in the document itself.

The CIA's assessment was cautious. The memo concludes the sighting can probably be explained as steep-climbing aircraft or missiles, and that the evidence was not solid enough to conclude the Soviets had developed a radically new type of aircraft. In other words, the agency treated the report as an ordinary phenomenon rather than as confirmation of anything extraordinary.

The memorandum is dated 1 November 1955, drafted the previous day (31 October 1955), and signed by H. H. Scoville, Jr. of the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence (OSI), the branch that analysed foreign scientific and technical developments.

Rather than being blacked out, the main difficulty with this record is legibility: the scanned text is heavily degraded, so several passages are hard to read and some details had to be reconstructed. Little appears to be formally redacted, but the poor scan quality means some quotations should be checked against the original.
public_caveats: The account rests on a single debriefing of eyewitnesses watching from a moving train, with no corroborating instrument or radar data.
The scanned document is heavily degraded (poor OCR), so some quoted wording is a best-effort reconstruction and should be checked against the original scan.
The document is not heavily redacted; the main limitation is readability, not blacked-out passages.
Details such as the exact location (Azerbaijan / place names) come from war.gov's catalogue metadata, not from clearly legible text in the memo.
The CIA itself framed the sighting as likely aircraft or missiles — it does not confirm an unidentified or exotic craft.
